titre: The Split Brain of Sperry and Gazzaniga
accroche: Cutting the corpus callosum of an epileptic patient reveals two brains that act without talking to each other.
contenu_vulgarise:
A man stares at a point in the center of a screen. For a hundred milliseconds, the image of a box appears to the right of that point. “A box,” he says at once. The same image now appears to the left of the fixation point. He is asked what he saw. “Nothing,” he answers, even though his eyes did receive the image.

## Two Brains That No Longer Talk

This patient, designated by the initials W.J., is a veteran operated on in the early 1960s by the neurosurgeons Joseph Bogen and Philip Vogel for severe, uncontrollable epilepsy. The operation, a commissurotomy, cuts the corpus callosum, the bundle of fibers that connects the two hemispheres. It relieves the epilepsy. It also leaves these patients with two hemispheres that can no longer communicate directly.

Roger Sperry and his collaborator Michael Gazzaniga draw a precise protocol from this. It is not the eye used that determines which hemisphere receives the image. It is where it appears relative to the fixated point: the left visual field projects to the right hemisphere, the right visual field to the left hemisphere, through the crossing of fibers at the optic chiasm. In almost all right-handers, language sits almost exclusively in the left hemisphere. A study of 326 healthy subjects measured right-sided language dominance in only 4% of strongly right-handed people. This is why the right hemisphere, having seen the image, cannot name it: it lacks the verbal output. But when the patient is simply asked to point, the left hand, controlled by the right hemisphere, correctly indicates the object seen.

Each half of the brain thus keeps its own perceptions and its own learning, without the other knowing anything about it. Sperry receives the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1981 for this work.

## Sperry's Own Warning

His experiments fed, in popular culture, the idea of a “logical” left brain and a “creative” right brain, each governing a type of personality. Sperry knew about this drift, and named it himself in his own Nobel lecture: the left-right dichotomy of cognitive mode, he says, “is an idea with which it is very easy to get carried away.” In the normal state, he specifies, the two hemispheres “seem to work closely together as a unit, rather than one being active while the other stays idle.”

The discoverer of the phenomenon thus warns, from the very podium that honors his discovery, against the use that would be made of it. The dissociation he documented is real, but only in patients whose bridge between the two hemispheres has been cut. In an intact brain, it says nothing about a dominant personality type.

carte.punch: The discoverer of the split brain warned against the myth drawn from his discovery.
carte.idee: In patients whose corpus callosum has been cut, each hemisphere perceives and learns without the other knowing. Sperry, who documented this phenomenon, already warned in his Nobel speech that the “left brain / right brain” dichotomy was an idea easy to get carried away with.

quiz.question: In a split-brain patient, why can the right hemisphere not name an object placed in the left visual field, even though it did perceive it?
choix: Because the left eye transmits no information to the right hemisphere
Because vision is totally absent in the right hemisphere
Because language almost always sits in the left hemisphere, inaccessible without a corpus callosum
Because the right hemisphere retains no memory of what it perceives
quiz.explication: The right hemisphere does receive the image, and the left hand it controls can in fact point to it correctly. But in almost all right-handers, language production depends on the left hemisphere; without a corpus callosum to transmit the information, the right hemisphere simply cannot put it into words.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who performed the operation that cut patient W.J.'s corpus callosum?
choix: Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga, who were conducting the experiment
The neurosurgeons Joseph Bogen and Philip Vogel
A surgeon who remained anonymous in the 1981 publication
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the operation, a commissurotomy, was performed by the neurosurgeons Joseph Bogen and Philip Vogel, in the early 1960s, to treat severe, uncontrollable epilepsy.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In Sperry and Gazzaniga's protocol, what determines which hemisphere receives an image shown to the patient?
choix: The eye the patient uses to look at the screen
The hand with which the patient answers
Where the image appears relative to the fixated point
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that it is not the eye used that determines which hemisphere receives the image, but where it appears relative to the fixation point, because of the crossing of fibers at the optic chiasm.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the study of 326 healthy subjects, cited in the entry, reveal?
choix: That right-sided language dominance concerns only 4% of strongly right-handed people
That half of right-handers have language housed in the right hemisphere
That language is never present in the right hemisphere
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The study of 326 healthy subjects measures language dominance in the right hemisphere in only 4% of strongly right-handed people, confirming that language almost always sits on the left, without excluding it entirely.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Sperry himself say, in his 1981 Nobel lecture, about the normal functioning of the two hemispheres?
choix: That they function completely independently of each other
That they work closely together as a unit
That only the left hemisphere is active in daily life
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sperry specifies in his Nobel lecture that, in the normal state, the two hemispheres seem to work closely together as a unit, rather than one being active while the other stays idle.
